Cardiovascular Disease in Women the Two Decades Following Uteroplacental Disorders: A Population-Based Data-Linkage Study

Burger RJ, Kalkman DN, Gordijn SJ et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Population-based retrospective cohort study (data linkage; Dutch perinatal registry and national hospital admissions, 2000–2022).
Key Question: What are the incidence and timing of premature cardiovascular disease (CVD) after different uteroplacental disorders, to guide timing and content of postpartum cardiovascular follow-up?
Key Findings:
  • Among 1,669,681 nulliparous women, any uteroplacental disorder was associated with increased overall CVD risk (aHR 1.70, 95% CI 1.67–1.74; median follow-up 11 years).
  • Hazard ratios were similar after PIH, pre-eclampsia, FGR and fetal death; risk after spontaneous preterm birth was less elevated.
  • Relative risk was highest soon after pregnancy but remained elevated beyond 10 years. Hypertension predominated after HDP; atherosclerosis after FGR. Socioeconomic factors had limited impact.
Clinical Relevance: Supports early cardiovascular risk assessment after all uteroplacental disorders, not only pre-eclampsia, which is relevant to UK postnatal and primary care follow-up pathways that currently focus largely on hypertensive disorders.
Limitations: Observational registry linkage using hospital admissions data may miss community-managed CVD and risks residual confounding; absolute risks are not reported in the abstract.

BJOG

Epidural in Labour and Obstetric Anal Sphincter Injury Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

Idzes D, Atkinson J, Gordon H et al. · 2026 Nov 08
Study Type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (86 studies, predominantly observational; N = 9,826,330 women).
Key Question: Is epidural analgesia in labour associated with a change in the risk of obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI)?
Key Findings:
  • Epidural use was associated with 15% lower odds of OASI overall (aOR 0.85, 95% CI 0.80–0.91; n = 9,302,188).
  • Among nulliparous women, the association was stronger: aOR 0.77 (95% CI 0.71–0.83; n = 1,083,923), a 23% reduction.
  • Pooled estimates were adjusted for clinical confounders; the abstract does not report heterogeneity or a separate RCT-only estimate.
Clinical Relevance: Reassuringly, epidural analgesia does not appear to increase OASI risk and may be modestly protective, which is useful for antenatal counselling and OASI-reduction discussions in UK units.
Limitations: Evidence is largely observational, so confounding (e.g. by indication) cannot be excluded and causality is not established, as the authors acknowledge.

Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Modern Treatment Modalities for Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis

Randombage PJS, Akurugodagama MS · 2026 Nov 08
Study Type: Systematic review and frequentist class-level network meta-analysis of RCTs (24 trial families, 4958 participants; primary symptom NMA 15 families, 3415 participants).
Key Question: What is the comparative efficacy and safety of treatments for genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM)?
Key Findings:
  • Local vaginal oestrogen was the only class with a CI excluding the null versus placebo/sham/control (SMD 0.34, 95% CI 0.02–0.66); prasterone (0.37), hyaluronic acid (0.31), ospemifene (0.24), moisturisers (0.15) and CO2 laser (0.03) all had CIs crossing zero.
  • Rankings were unstable (P-scores identical for oestrogen and prasterone at 0.704); heterogeneity was material (I² 65.6%).
  • CINeMA confidence was low for oestrogen and prasterone versus control, and very low for the other 19 comparisons.
Clinical Relevance: Supports local vaginal oestrogen as first-line GSM treatment and cautions against positioning laser or radiofrequency as equivalent or superior, relevant to NHS use of energy-based devices and individualised stepped care.
Limitations: Evidence quality is weak: 11 of 24 trial families were at high risk of bias, imprecision was marked, and radiofrequency was excluded from the primary NMA for lack of extractable data.

BJOG

Postpartum Perineal Assessment After Vaginal Birth and Detection of Obstetric Anal Sphincter Injury: A Scoping Review

Ratto C, Sultan AH, Fernando R et al. · 2026 Nov 08
Study Type: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) with AGREE II appraisal of formal guidelines.
Key Question: How do international guidelines and supporting evidence address postpartum perineal assessment and detection of obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI)?
Key Findings:
  • 14 core guidelines, 3 regional documents and 31 evidence sources were included.
  • All guidelines covered immediate postpartum perineal assessment, but recommendations differed considerably on digital rectal examination, role and timing of imaging, diagnostic escalation and structured follow-up.
  • Guidance on implementation (documentation, training, audit/quality improvement) was inconsistent. The abstract reports no AGREE II scores or quantitative findings.
Clinical Relevance: Given that OASI is under-recognised, UK units may wish to review local pathways for reassessment, imaging access and audit against these identified gaps, as national guidance may not resolve them.
Limitations: As a scoping review, it maps rather than evaluates evidence quality or outcomes, so it cannot indicate which approaches best improve OASI detection.

Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology

Early third-trimester maternal cardiac function and morphometry in high-risk pregnancies that subsequently developed fetal growth restriction and/or pre-eclampsia

Martinez-Egea J, Daza M, Pumarola C et al. · 2026 Nov 08
Study Type: Prospective cohort study (single centre, Barcelona; n=948)
Key Question: Do maternal cardiac function and morphology at 27+0 to 28+6 weeks differ in high-risk pregnancies that subsequently develop FGR and/or pre-eclampsia (PE) compared with those that remain uncomplicated?
Key Findings:
  • Pregnancies later affected by FGR (±PE; n=59) or isolated PE (n=70) had lower stroke volume (59.7 and 61.1 vs 64.2 mL) and BMI-indexed cardiac output, with higher systemic vascular resistance (1393 and 1339 vs 1252 dynes·s/cm⁵) than uncomplicated pregnancies (n=819). FGR and PE were independently associated with lower CO and higher SVR after BMI adjustment.
  • The FGR phenotype showed smaller LV end-diastolic diameter (4.27 vs 4.48 cm), suggesting reduced preload, without tachycardia.
  • Isolated PE showed higher MAP and heart rate, with greater LV wall thickness (relative wall thickness 0.45 vs 0.42).
Clinical Relevance: Maternal echocardiography may support early phenotype-specific risk stratification in high-risk pregnancies, though this is not yet part of UK routine care.
Limitations: Differences between groups are modest, with no predictive performance data (e.g., AUC, detection rates) reported, and the findings are from a single-centre, selected high-risk population.

American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

Baclofen Vaginal Suppositories in Chronic Pelvic Pain: a Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo Controlled Trial

Rothenberger RW, Abraham A, Gaskins JT et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (single-centre status not stated).
Key Question: Do nightly 20 mg baclofen vaginal suppositories reduce pelvic floor muscle tenderness in women with chronic pelvic pain compared with placebo?
Key Findings:
  • Primary outcome (pelvic floor palpation VAS, 8 weeks): median improvement 33.5 mm with baclofen vs 7.2 mm with placebo (p<0.001), exceeding the 20 mm MCID.
  • Patient-reported overall pain VAS improved by a median of 32.0 mm vs 0.0 mm (p=0.001). PROMIS pain interference, global health and sexual function showed no significant between-group differences.
  • No adverse events with baclofen; two minor events (headache, vaginal irritation) in the placebo arm.
Clinical Relevance: Offers a potential locally delivered treatment for myofascial pelvic pain, though baclofen vaginal suppositories are unlicensed in the UK and would require specials compounding.
Limitations: Small sample (37 randomised) with only 8 weeks' follow-up, and no significant improvement in function or quality-of-life measures.

American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

Urgency urinary incontinence, one condition, or many? Cluster analysis of physiological variables in the Symptoms of Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network (LURN) II cohort

DeLancey JOL, Andreev VP, Andrews C et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Exploratory secondary cohort analysis (LURN II) using consensus cluster analysis; 56 women with UUI, 31 asymptomatic controls.
Key Question: Can women with urgency urinary incontinence (UUI) be separated into physiologically distinct phenotypes using bladder and urethral motor and sensory testing?
Key Findings:
  • Three clusters emerged from 32 urodynamic and sensory variables. Cluster A (n=15) had detrusor overactivity with and without lidocaine, and reduced sensation volumes (39–55% of controls) with normal urethral function.
  • Cluster B (n=18) showed a 138 mL (72%) capacity increase after intravesical lidocaine and a 30% reduction in maximum urethral closure pressure. Cluster C (n=23) showed minimal lidocaine response and little detrusor overactivity.
  • Demographics and symptoms were similar across clusters, so the phenotypes cannot be distinguished clinically. Discriminating variables had AUCs of 0.83–0.95.
Clinical Relevance: UUI may comprise mechanistically distinct conditions, which could explain variable treatment response, but cluster-specific management remains hypothetical and not applicable to current NHS practice.
Limitations: Small sample with no external validation, and AUCs are likely optimistic as the predictors were derived from the same variables that defined the clusters.

BJOG

Perioperative Morbidity and Recurrence After One-Stage Laparoscopic Resection for Multicompartment Deep Endometriosis: A Multicentre Cohort Study

Pagano F, Sík PB, Imboden S et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Retrospective multicentre cohort study (two tertiary endometriosis centres; n=299).
Key Question: What are the perioperative morbidity and recurrence rates after one-stage laparoscopic resection of multicompartment deep endometriosis, and which factors predict complications?
Key Findings:
  • Clavien-Dindo ≥II complications occurred in 11.7% (35/299); ≥IIIb in 4.7% (14/299).
  • Each additional #ENZIAN compartment involved independently increased odds of clinically relevant complications (aOR 1.51, 95% CI 1.04–2.18).
  • Documented recurrence was 14.4% (43/299), with 8.7% (26/299) reoperated; recurrence-free survival did not differ by bowel (p=0.431) or bladder (p=0.116) surgical technique.
Clinical Relevance: Supports using overall anatomical extent (#ENZIAN) in consent and surgical planning, reinforcing referral of multicompartment disease to BSGE-accredited centres.
Limitations: Retrospective design with follow-up data for only 77.3% of patients, so recurrence rates are likely underestimated and technique comparisons may be underpowered.
